transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I’m Dr. [Name]. What brings you in today?

Um, yeah… I guess what finally made me call EAP was this thing at work where every little bang just, like, sets me off. A file drawer slams or someone drops a coffee mug, and I jump hard—way more than I should. 

And then my chest keeps racing for a while after, which is embarrassing, honestly. I supervise a sales team, so I’m supposed to be the calm one, you know? But lately even normal office noises have me reacting like something terrible just happened.
Can you think of any specific incident or event that might have triggered this reaction to sounds? Like something that happened around the time this started?

Yeah, um… I think it started after this late-night confrontation with my regional boss. It’s been about two weeks now.

Which is weird, because I’ve had tense meetings before, you know? Sales is basically just people being tense in button-down shirts half the time. But that night was different somehow, and since then the sound thing has been happening.
Can you tell me more about that confrontation with your regional boss? Did you feel intense fear, helplessness, or horror during or after it?

I mean… it was intense, yeah, but I don’t know if I’d use those exact words. Fear, helplessness, horror—those sound kind of dramatic, and maybe I’m being weird about admitting that.

He was really in my face about numbers and performance, and I remember feeling… cornered, I guess? But then I also keep thinking, like, plenty of people get yelled at by bosses and they don’t end up sitting in a doctor’s office over it. My old manager used to do these “motivational” talks that were basically just public shaming with a PowerPoint, so part of me is like, maybe I should be used to it.

So… I’m not sure. It upset me a lot, but I don’t know how to label it.
Since that confrontation with your boss, have you noticed yourself avoiding certain situations, feeling more negative or numb, or having trouble concentrating?

Yeah, the concentrating part, definitely. Like at work I’ll open Salesforce to check my reps’ notes, and then I realize I’ve just been staring at the same account for, I don’t know, ten minutes. Not even reading it, really.

And then simple stuff feels harder than it should. Like deciding who should cover a client visit—normally that’s just a quick call, I do it all day—but lately I sort of freeze on it. Which is annoying because my team already acts like Salesforce is this giant monster, and I’m usually the one saying, “No, just document the activity properly,” and now I’m the one sitting there lost in it.
Since that confrontation with your boss, have you found yourself being more on edge or watchful, like you’re always waiting for something bad to happen?

Yeah… I guess I have, now that you say it that way.

Like when I’m in the office, I keep sort of tracking where my boss is. Not in a normal “oh, he’s in a meeting” way, more like I notice if he walks past the glass doors or if I hear his voice down the hall. And I keep checking where the exits are, which is stupid because I know the layout—I’ve worked there long enough.

I’ll be supposed to be focused on my team, you know, looking at pipeline stuff or helping somebody figure out an account, and instead I’m aware of whether someone’s coming up behind me. Like I don’t want to be surprised. It makes me feel ridiculous, honestly.
Since that incident with your boss, have you noticed yourself feeling more down, irritable, or detached from people, even when you're not at work?

Yeah… I mean, I’m still doing stuff. Like I still go to beach volleyball, because if I don’t go then everyone texts me like, “Where are you?” and it becomes this whole thing. And I had a couple friends over for dinner last weekend—I made this pasta thing I’ve made a million times.

But it’s weird, because normally that would feel good, you know? Like I’d be into the game, or joking around while cooking, and now it’s more like I’m just… present. Doing the steps. Serving food, making conversation, showing up.

It doesn’t really land as fun or satisfying the way it usually would. I don’t know if that’s “detached,” exactly, but it feels kind of like I’m going through the motions.
Since that incident with your boss, have you found yourself feeling persistently down, hopeless, or detached from others, even when you're not at work?

Yeah, kind of. I wouldn’t say hopeless exactly, but detached, yeah.

Like I still go to beach volleyball, and I had a couple friends over for dinner last weekend—actually I made this pasta I always make, which usually people ask for, and I normally get into the whole cooking thing, like timing everything and making it nice. But this time it was just… steps. Boil water, sauce, plates, talk when I’m supposed to talk.

Same with volleyball. I’m there, I’m playing, people are joking around, and I’m sort of doing the motions, but it doesn’t really feel fun or satisfying the way it normally does. It’s like I’m present, but not really getting anything from it.

Since that confrontation with your boss, have you found yourself having trouble remembering important parts of the event, or feeling negative about yourself, like you’re to blame or that you should have done something differently?

Yeah… that part is weird. I remember certain things really clearly, like him slamming the chair and then standing in front of the door. Like that’s stuck in my head.

But when I try to tell someone the worst part—like the actual words he said to me—it’s just… blank. Which is frustrating, because I know that was the part that messed with me the most. It’s like that section got cut out.

And then I start second-guessing myself, like maybe I’m explaining it badly or making it sound less serious than it was. I don’t know. I keep getting stuck there.
Since that incident with your boss, have you found yourself feeling persistently down, hopeless, or detached from others, even when you're not at work?

Yeah… I think detached is probably the best word. Not hopeless, exactly. I mean, I’m still doing things.

Like I still go to beach volleyball—though honestly last time I kept thinking about how one of the guys always brings this terrible portable speaker and plays the same playlist every week, which normally makes me laugh, but even that was just kind of… there. And I had a couple friends over for dinner last weekend, made pasta, did the whole thing.

But it didn’t feel like anything. I was playing, cooking, talking, whatever, but it was more like I was following steps than actually enjoying it. Normally those are the things that reset me, and lately it’s like none of it really lands as fun or satisfying.
